definition: showy; designed to impress or attract notice
memoryTip: OSTENTatious — put on a show (like a gold tent) so everyone stares.
correctPassage: Ostentatious displays of wealth sat uneasily with the town's modest culture.
wrongPassages: She preferred an ostentatious desk in the back corner where no visitor would notice her.
The password was deliberately ostentatious so that anyone could guess it on the first try.
His ostentatious notes filled three pages with nothing but blank lines and a title.

memoryTip: Conjecture = a guess — conjectural claims rest on guesswork, not proof.
correctPassage: Any claim about the author's motives remains largely conjectural.
wrongPassages: The lab's conjectural measurements matched the certified reference sample exactly.
Her conjectural diary listed every appointment she had already confirmed in writing.
The jury accepted only conjectural evidence: fingerprints, video, and a signed confession.

memoryTip: String-tight rules — pulled taut; no slack allowed.
correctPassage: Stringent safety standards apply to every chemical in the lab.
wrongPassages: The dress code was so stringent that students could wear anything they liked.
His stringent schedule left whole afternoons free with no tasks assigned.
Editors praised the draft for its stringent arguments full of vague, unsupported claims.

memoryTip: Ego-tistical: the ego is the star of every sentence.
correctPassage: An egotistical refusal to share credit damaged team morale.
wrongPassages: Her egotistical mentoring always put the interns' growth ahead of her own reputation.
The egotistical volunteer stayed late scrubbing floors no one else would touch.
Critics called the memoir egotistical for focusing entirely on other people's achievements.

memoryTip: Pliant ≈ pliable — bends without breaking; yields to pressure.
correctPassage: Young stems are pliant enough to train along a trellis.
wrongPassages: The pliant steel beam refused to flex even under the crane's full load.
A pliant negotiator never changed position no matter how strong the counteroffer.
The judge was so pliant that no lawyer could sway her from the written law.
